lessons.title: Why and how fruit is treated after harvest
lessons.html:
Postharvest treatments

Fruit for export may spend four to six weeks or more between packing and the consumer. To survive this, many fruit kinds receive postharvest treatments in the packhouse. Typical purposes are:

  • Decay control: fungicides or sanitisers reduce moulds such as green and blue mould on citrus.
  • Moisture loss control and shine: waxes or coatings, mainly on citrus and some apples.
  • Storage disorder control: for example treatments applied to some apple and pear cultivars to reduce storage disorders, as approved for the market.
  • Cleaning: washing and brushing to remove dirt, sooty mould and residues.

Application methods

MethodDescription
DrenchBins are drenched with treatment solution before entering the line
Dip tank / bathFruit passes through a tank of solution, often heated
Spray bar / flooderSolution is sprayed over fruit on brushes
Wax applicatorWax is sprayed onto fruit on rotating brushes, followed by a drying tunnel
Fumigation / gas treatmentDone in sealed rooms by trained, authorised persons only

Legal and market controls

Only products registered under Act 36 of 1947 for that use may be applied, at the label dose. In addition, each export market sets its own maximum residue limits (MRLs) and lists of permitted active ingredients. The technical or QC manager decides the treatment programme for each market, and the operator must apply exactly that programme. Never change the product or concentration on your own.

Critical parameters

A treatment only works if key parameters stay within limits: concentration, temperature (for heated baths), contact time (line speed or drench time), pH for some products, coverage of all fruit, and solution cleanliness. Dirty, overused solutions lose effectiveness and can spread spores instead of killing them.

lessons.title: Monitoring, recording and acting on deviations
lessons.html:
The monitor's job

The person monitoring treatments checks that the process runs within its limits, records evidence, and acts when it does not.

Start-up checks

  1. Confirm the treatment programme for the batch and market.
  2. Check that the correct products are in the mixing area and labels match.
  3. Verify that tanks were cleaned and filled to the correct volume.
  4. Check that solutions were mixed at the specified concentration, recorded with product batch numbers and quantities.
  5. Check heaters, pumps, nozzles, brushes and agitation are working.

During the run

  • Measure concentration at the set intervals using the approved method (for example test kits, titration or lab samples), and top up or replace solution as the procedure says.
  • Check temperature and pH where required.
  • Check line speed for correct contact time.
  • Watch spray patterns: blocked nozzles leave fruit untreated.
  • Watch wax coverage and drying: fruit should leave the tunnel dry, not sticky.
  • Check the solution for dirt and debris. Change it according to the schedule or volume treated.

Records

Record every check with time, reading, batch or producer, and your initials. Records prove to auditors and buyers that the fruit was treated correctly, and are needed for traceability.

Deviations

If any reading falls outside limits, act immediately:

  1. Inform the supervisor or technical manager.
  2. Correct the cause if authorised (adjust, top up, unblock nozzles).
  3. Identify which fruit was affected, from what time, so it can be held, retreated or redirected as management decides.
  4. Record the deviation and the action taken.

Over-dosing is as serious as under-dosing, because residues may exceed the market's MRL and a consignment may be rejected.

Safety and environment

  • Wear the PPE on the product label: chemical-resistant gloves, goggles or face shield, apron and boots, and a respirator where required.
  • Mix chemicals in a ventilated, bunded area. Add product to water as the label directs.
  • Never enter fumigation rooms or areas under gas treatment unless trained and authorised.
  • Dispose of spent solutions only through the approved system, never into drains or the veld.
  • Know the first aid steps on the label and where the eyewash and shower are.

Key points

  • Treatments control decay, water loss and some storage disorders.
  • Use only registered products and the programme set for each market.
  • Monitor concentration, temperature, contact time, pH, coverage and cleanliness.
  • Record every check and report deviations immediately, identifying affected fruit.
  • Wear label PPE and dispose of spent solutions correctly.
